Just last summer, I got into making spreadsheets for random data sets, and taught myself how to use Apps Scripts on Google Sheets, which is basically a way to implement JavaScript into your Google Sheet in order to do more complicated functions. 

My favorite spreadsheet that I have made is a sort of “mock SIS,” in which I created a database with around 500 courses that are currently offered by Tufts (including information about what attributes they have, number of credits, typical semesters run, etc.). Then, in various different tabs, I programmed a way to create a new schedule or upload an old one, see if that schedule fulfills my major and minor requirements, and store that schedule for later use.

To build the project, I started off quite simply, trying to do as much of the code as I could with the provided functions within Google Sheets. As I did, I made a list of functions I could not make, and then proceeded to program those ones using Apps Scripts. Finally, I made the sheets aesthetically pleasing and added conditional formatting.

The most challenging part of this project was definitely the code itself. I was still relatively new to JavaScript and Apps Scripts when I began it, so I had to teach myself as I went, much like the coding we do in JumboCode. Another challenging – and less expected – issue I ran into was the efficiency of my code. Because there are so many tabs in the spreadsheet and so many functions, I often found that my code was running too slowly so I needed to find ways to make it simpler and less expensive.

After struggling to find the time to cook healthy, balanced meals while managing the busy life of school, I had an idea for a personal project. In the weeks between my summer job and school starting, I developed an mobile app called "CookNook", a cross-platform mobile app for cataloging personal recipes that enables users to generate recipes from user-provided ingredients through a custom OpenAI API endpoint. The idea behind the app was to create a place where I could save all my recipes, as well as generate recipes based on whatever ingredients I had lying around in the fridge. 

I built the app by first implementing the basic front-end interface using React Native and Expo, then implementing the back-end using Firebase and Node.js, and finally connecting the two. I used Git/Github for version control throughout. I had very little experience with React Native, so this was challenging. However, with time, effort, and the occasional late-night tutorial sessions, I was able to slowly improve. Additionally, this was my first experience with designing my own tech stack. I spent a lot of time researching different technologies, choosing ones that best fit my project, and then figuring out how to implement them into the project. While this process was frustrating at times, it improved my ability to understand documentation and choose certain technologies for a specific task.

In the end, building CookNook was incredibly rewarding. I was able to create a functional app that solved a problem I personally experienced, and the project gave me a deeper understanding of mobile development, back-end integration, and using AI to enhance user experiences. Coming out of CS11 last semester, I was eager to keep coding and to make a project of my own. Early in the summer, my mom expressed to me her frustration at work - as a scientist, one of her responsibilities was manually sorting through over 700 source racks containing lab samples and re-distributing them into destination racks. There were several constraints that made the problem tedious and and time-consuming - for example, each source rack held a random amount of samples ranging from 0 to 96, and she was required to work in batches of 20 racks at a time. The 20 racks in a batch could be split into any combination of source and destination racks she wanted (ex. 19 source + 1 destination, or 17 source + 3 destination), which added a layer of complexity. Hearing this, I decided that I would create a C++ program that could take in rack data, efficiently distribute the racks, and output the results to a csv file, in order to help save my mom from future headaches.

I am proud of this project because I was able to apply my limited knowledge of C++ and object-oriented programming to create a fully functional program that stored data in an efficient way.  I won’t get into the nitty gritty details, but my program implemented a Source Rack class, a Batch class containing a vector to add Source Racks to, and an array holding the sample frequencies of the Source Racks (the number of source racks containing 1 sample, 2 samples, 3 samples, etc). The solution relied on mathematical analysis of the sample frequencies array to build the batches one by one. It would try out different source racks to add to the current batch, with the goal of filling the destination rack(s) as completely as possible while minimizing the total number of batches, switching strategies when the current one didn't seem to be working out.

Through this project, I gained a lot of practice planning, testing, and debugging. I also had to do my own research on concepts not taught in CS11, like handling C++ exceptions. Perhaps the most difficult part was translating my human decision process into code - for example, isolating what factors indicate that a strategy is not working so that the program could detect this and move onto a different strategy (without me directly telling it to). I found that the best way to deal with complex coding problems like this was to write a clear, detailed implementation plan. I consider my work to have paid off in the end, especially after seeing the genuine look of appreciation my mom had when I presented her with my solution. I helped make her life easier, and I hope to continue helping others through JumboCode!

One project I'm particularly proud of is Zap! from CS15. For this project, I implemented Huffman coding to compress and decompress text files.

I built the program by constructing a Huffman tree. Huffman coding is a lossless compression algorithm that builds a binary tree where more frequent characters have shorter paths from the root, and less frequent characters have longer paths. I started by creating nodes for the two lowest-frequency characters and combined them into a parent node. I continued this process until there were only two parent nodes left, which I then joined to form the root. The tree is designed so that the path from the root to less frequent letters is longer, while more frequent letters have shorter paths, ensuring that we use the least number of bits to encode the text.

The most challenging part of this project was figuring out the right traversal method for serializing and deserializing the Huffman tree. This step was critical for accurately reconstructing the tree during decompression and ensuring that the encoded text could be correctly decoded. To solve this, I had to ensure that I understood the different binary tree traversal methods and pay close attention to how the Huffman tree was built. I'm a visual learner, and so pictures of trees and traversal paths were a great help, as well as office hours and lecture slides, which ultimately helped me figure out a variation of pre-order traversal algorithm to serialize and deserialize the Huffman tree to accomplish he compression and decompression.

column16:
The project I’m most proud of was my CS Internal Assessment coding project in senior year. Quickly, the IA is simple: find a client, their problem, and use computer science techniques to build a solution. My client was my uncle, who was trying to improve his golf swing by visually comparing his golf swing video to that of some PGA professional, trying to eyeball discrepancies between the two. He wanted a more consistent, accurate, and precise way to compare the two swings to gain useful insight. I took this and wanted to build an app that could in some way “quantify” a golf swing and output numbers that could tell the user information.
This goes pretty in depth, but just wanted to demonstrate my thought processes about the challenges and the actual algorithms.
Using a concept we had been learning about in the IB CS Case Study and through Google’s MediaPipe API, I managed to get a green dot that would track each part of a subject’s body in a video, which is known as Human Pose Estimation. Once the body part key points could be tracked, the fact that each could be represented on a 2D coordinate plane helped me to begin building the statistics. Taking only videos from straight behind the golfer, some of the simpler stats would be something like initial knee bend angle, or initial back angle, which were simply found by discerning the angle between three points in space. One of the most complex statistics to calculate was one that I called top-arm angle, which was essentially the angle at which the golfer’s front arm would make with a horizontal line along the golfer’s shoulder at the moment the wrists were at the highest point of the golf swing. However, you cannot just track the y-values of the wrist and find the max over the entire video, because the follow through is almost always higher than the takeback. Similarly, you can’t solve that problem by taking the second-highest, because it’s very likely that the second highest is also in the follow through. The solution was not perfect, but it worked essentially every time with a video submitted at iPhone slo-mo speed. Using a Python class I built called peakFinder, the current coordinates of the wrist would be constantly stored at each frame of the video until they began to increase (meaning move back down the screen, or when the max point would have already happened). Once this happened, a count threshold variable would begin counting frames that the y-value continued to move down the screen, and once thirty frames had passed it would conclude that the highest point was that last stored maximum. If, at any point, the wrist started going back up, the threshold variable would reset. It wasn’t perfect, however, because often the golfer would move their hands ever so slightly up and down at the beginning of the swing and throw the threshold variable past 30. I added another condition to prevent this: the max wrist value had to be more than 200 pixels above the wrist value in the first frame, making sure it was actually at the top of the swing. I also found success in tracking a stat that would measure how much horizontal shift had taken place in the wrists from the beginning of the swing to when the wrists were at the waist. For example, Rory McIlroy’s number here was 10 pixels forward; Collin Morikawa’s was 10 backward. Mine was 112 forward, so safe to say I had found some useful discrepancy. 
Using OOP in Python, these statistics were all assembled and then compared, in a TKinter GUI for the user, with the same statistics for Rory McIlroy, and then a “Similarity Score” was created with Pearson’s Correlation Coefficient. The score was saved in a SQL database with the user’s name, score, and date, so that their progress could be observed. Overall, in addition to learning so much more about Human Pose Estimation, SQL queries and tables, OOP, and Python in general, I took away how valuable it is to plan out the concept of how an algorithm will work, like the top-arm angle, before ever coding. The fun, for me, was the conceptual problem solving and trying to make something that actually worked. At the end, I submitted my golf swing and the program gave me a 61/100. I chose another pro at random, Collin Morikawa, and submitted a video of his swing. The program scored him a 99.5/100. In some way or another, reasonable analysis was taking place.

column16: The project that I am proud of is decomposing a monolithic messaging backend into containerized microservices deployed on Amazon EKS. While working as a backend developer in the industry, the product's entire messaging backend was a monolith with lots of interdependent features. As the company grew, such monolithic architecture presented significant challenges in supporting increased read-and-write traffic and incorporating new features. Driven by the discovery that few interdependent features in the monolith were tied to messaging functionalities, I explored the possibility of breaking down the monolith into multiple self-contained services. This investigation ultimately introduced me to a concept known as microservices. After collaborating with all messaging teams for 16 months, our team successfully transformed our message backend into a distributed system where features are independently deployable microservices that communicate over a network. Our contributions have thus provided our messaging backend with greater flexibility and scalability.

I'm proud of the IoT Kitchen project I created, which was designed to enhance the cooking experience for amateur home cooks. The project utilized Google Firebase for real-time data storage, Java for backend development, RFID tags to manage inventory, Arduino for sensor integration, and Natural Language Processing (NLP) to enable interactive voice commands. This project was done in collaboration with a client from General Electric.

The goal was to create a seamless and interactive cooking assistant that could guide users through recipes, suggest meals based on available ingredients, and manage kitchen inventory. One of the biggest challenges was integrating multiple technologies to work together smoothly, especially the real-time data synchronization between Firebase, Arduino sensors, and the Java backend. Additionally, training the NLP model to accurately understand user commands in a noisy kitchen environment required extensive testing and refinement.

Through this project, I not only strengthened my skills in IoT development, software integration, and machine learning but also learned the importance of iterative testing and user feedback. It was exciting to see how these technologies could come together to create a user-friendly solution that could have real-world applications.

This summer I worked with a group of Tufts students to develop a website for a platform called ‘Puppy AI’. Puppy AI is a series of lessons centered around the LEGO SPIKE that teach students the basic concepts of reinforcement learning. When I joined the team they had already developed the lessons and built a very basic website. Thus, my primary role became front-end development for the site. 

We used raw HTML, CSS, and JS to build the website. We stored everything (code, images, icons, etc) in a GitHub repository and committed to the repository via VS Code through GitHub Desktop. The project was unique because all of the code that we had to run on the SPIKE was in Python. Thus, we used Micro Python to embed and run Python files and Python editors in the page. 

Many technical challenges arose due to the two-way communication challenges between the site and the SPIKE itself. We also struggled to enable Bluetooth functionality. Working primarily on the front-end development, I faced many redesigns after we tested the website on students in the area and also on my coworkers. In particular there was a code editor portion of the website that took a while to build as all of its features needed to be clear to the user yet not too overwhelming to use. This was the first web dev project I had ever really done in a group so it was difficult at first to coordinate all of our commits to the repository. However, once we started to communicate more it became very fun to be able to bounce ideas off of my teammates!

column16: A project that really excited me was the Gerp project in CS15: Data Structures. The project task was to create a program that given a file directory, could query the directory for user-inputted words. It needed to be able to search in case-sensitive and insensitive. The project excited me because of its complexity - to build it, my teammate and I represented the file directory as a tree. We then parsed through this tree, storing each word of each file as a key in a HashMap that mapped words to their occurrences (line #, directory, and line) within the file system. The biggest challenge I faced was with duplicate capitalization words on the same line during case-insensitive search - our program incorrectly printed duplicate lines for the different capitalizations of the same word on the same line. We ultimately solved this using a Set and storing all the file#, line# as pairs within this set, then reprinting manually the lines using this set. Apart from this, it was just an amazing and exciting challenge to think of the numerous project parts - a 2D vector to represent files and their lines, a giant HashMap of words, a file tree, etc. But ultimately, it was my most proud programming project ever since it was quite complex and so rewarding when it finally worked out in the end. My partner (Jennifer Luo, PM of English at Large) and I had so much fun working together on this project.

column16:
One project that really excited me was an interactive art installation I developed called By The Car Window. The goal of the project was to create an immersive experience where users could interact with a digital environment through hand gestures. I led the entire development process, utilizing TouchDesigner, Python, and UltraLeap technology to bring it to life.

The core of the installation involved using Leap Motion sensors to track users' hand movements. I designed a motion-tracking system that captured these gestures in real-time, allowing users to interact with an illustrated car window environment. As users moved their hands, they could manipulate objects outside the car window—such as changing the weather or adjusting the landscape—creating a dynamic, personalized experience.

One of the major challenges was ensuring precise hand-tracking and smooth interaction. Leap Motion sensors can be sensitive, and I had to fine-tune the system to avoid lag and ensure that every gesture translated accurately on the screen. Additionally, I had to balance the aesthetic aspects with the technical demands, making sure that the visuals and interactions felt natural and engaging while maintaining performance.

Ultimately, this project was a rewarding challenge because it merged art, technology, and interaction in a way that captivated users and pushed me to refine my skills in both creative coding and interactive design.

The LGBTQ Senior Housing project resonates with me because it addresses the unique economic and social challenges faced by LGBTQ seniors, many of whom have led the fight for LGBTQ rights. The progress made—whether legalizing same-sex marriage or securing workplace protections—rests on the shoulders of these elders. I feel a responsibility to honor their contributions by ensuring they have access to safe, affordable housing. LGBTQ seniors often face discrimination, isolation, and lack of family support, making welcoming and inclusive housing vital. What excites me about this project isn't just about providing housing but also creating a space for connection and community building.

The New England Innocence Project (NEIP) also stands out. Their work in correcting wrongful convictions addresses systemic issues in the criminal justice system that disproportionately affects marginalized groups. Wrongful arrests often stem from racial bias, socioeconomic inequality, and inadequate legal representation. NEIP’s work to exonerate individuals requires immense data, coordination, and time. I believe technology has the power to be a step in solving these social issues, and building an exoneree database that streamlines client management for the NEIP could make a huge difference in their advocacy work.

The English at Large project draws me in due to its focus on helping immigrants improve their English skills. As someone from a Filipino immigrant household, I’ve seen how challenging it can be to learn a second language, especially when it’s essential for navigating everyday life, from securing employment to simply feeling a sense of belonging in a new country. My family’s experience has shown me how language barriers can create feelings of isolation. That’s why I’m passionate about initiatives like this, which aim to reduce those barriers and open up new opportunities for immigrants. Helping to build a system that supports this mission resonates with me on a personal level.

Overall I would be extremely appreciative to join any of these initiatives or projects. I am deeply passionate about social work and hope to be a part of supporting a community in any way I can. I would be extremely appreciative to join any project and hope I can contribute my skills effectively.

column16:
I believe in mental health awareness, specifically destigmatizing self-care such as psychotherapy, journaling, and meditation. During the pandemic, I was startled by the lack of access and recognition for mental health resources. Mental health struggles are real, and, contrary to public belief, they affect everyone. 

To address this issue, I developed a journaling program, Therabot, using Java and JavaFX. Beyond offering custom journaling prompts, Therabot stores the mood score, or self-reported mood change, from each journaling session in an encrypted, local file and reports insights from that statistic using an artificial intelligence-based algorithm. Therabot received first place in the Orange County Science and Engineering Fair, but I knew that its potential extended further. I immediately contacted my school’s administration to orchestrate mass test trials at my school. With overwhelmingly positive feedback, most testers improved their mood score but noted that the software would be more convenient on their phones. Thus, it was very important that I created Therabot!, the mobile application; however, this process did not come without challenges.

The biggest hurdle I climbed was adapting Therabot! for both Apple and Android, who maintain separate requirements. Java, JavaFX, GitHub, CSS, XML, Gluon Mobile, NetBeans, 
Eclipse, Ubuntu, Terminal, and Swift, most of which I was unfamiliar with prior to pursuing this project, made this mobile diversity possible. Without a mentor to help me learn these languages, I utilized YouTube along with public forums during the learning process. Initially, I had difficulty, but as my expertise grew, so did my patience. I am proud of myself for persevering because I was able to implement all the features I had hoped to include.

With accessibility at the forefront of this transition, the app is available for free and independent of Wi-Fi. Therabot! has received recognition from Congress and within the mental health community. The most valuable reward from this extensive project, however, has been the skills gained and lives touched along the way.

My experience in developing Therabot excites me because it demonstrates how computer science and education empower us to impact the world. I find it inspiring that coding allows us to positively impact our greater community and address topics that matter to us.

column16: When I was 17, I became the first person in the Smash Ultimate modding scene to add a completely new character to the game. At the time, Ultimate modding consisted mostly of replacing files for stuff like minor parameter changes and model swaps, and writing Rust plugins to hook and overwrite functions from the base game, letting us reimplement major mechanics like how the game handles ground collision, how it reads inputs, and individual move scripts. This approach to code editing gave us a lot of power since it effectively let any function be an entry point, and I wanted to test just how far we could push that, so I started adding a character. The main limitation I was working under was the fact that we couldn't actually add new files, only replace existing ones, meaning that in order to load the assets for a new character, I needed to put those assets inside of an existing character's files, load the existing character, and tell the game to use parts of the file which corresponded to whichever character the user actually wanted to play as. Doing this meant I had to put a hook on any function responsible for playing audio, starting an animation, changing the visibility of a mesh (this one in particular was very frustrating since the function in question was unnamed and needed to be accessed by offset), checking the value of a parameter, spawning particle effects, and executing move scripts. Since I was still teaching myself Rust at the time, keeping this code organized was definitely a challenge, and the project as a whole definitely had a lot of spaghetti code in it, but in the end I was successful, and the final result can be seen here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ft-fLCeOBQU

column16: In High School, I was part of schools Debate Team, and I remember that it was always difficult for the coach to make the team pairings for the tournaments. So, for my final project for AP Computer Science, I chose to write a program that would make the pairings for her for each round. It was very difficult for me to write the code because I had only been coding for a couple of months at this point and I only had a basic understanding of how to write programs, but every day I would write out a small goal for myself and I would do my best to get that part done. Sometimes I succeeded and sometimes I had to come back the next day and try again. I had made a class to represent each team and a class to represent each round. The biggest challenge I faced was figuring out a ranking system, as when teams progress in tournaments they must face other teams who have the same win to loss ration as them. I.e. after round 3 if a team won once and lost once, they can only face teams who had done the same. I had googled different methods I could use and tried to think through the edge case of what if there was an odd amount of teams who had the same win to loss ratio. Finally, I found a way to assign point values to each team and instated a condition that would start at the very top of the leaderboard and pair teams up that way. My most significant volunteer experience was with the Smart Border Coalition, where I dedicated over 350 hours to a project aimed at improving efficiency at the San Diego/Tijuana border. The core of my work involved developing two key components: a comprehensive database and a real-time dashboard.

During my senior year in high school, I took many CS courses at Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI). In one of my courses, CS 1102, we had to use Racket, a language that was very different than I was used to. It was based on LISP, which meant that all iterative processes were done using recursion and everything was based on lists. One of the hardest projects that I had to do in this class was a Tic-Tac-Toe game. In it, my partner and I had to implement a computer for the player to play against that utilized a minimax algorithm. Because of a combination of lack of experience with the algorithm, working with a new language, and 8 layers of recursive insanity, this ended up being the hardest project of that class.

Implementing player interaction was simple enough, but once we got to the minimax part of the project, we were at a roadblock. Every time we ran our code, it always seemed like we were one step off. The computer would suddenly fill the board with Os. We fixed that. Oops, the computer now played a whole entire game by itself. Ahh, silly computer, you have to only go one step in the tree, not all of them at once! 

After we were finally able to resolve what felt like countless bugs in our system and did our very last tests, we looked over our code again. What ultimately helped us finish this project was splitting everything into smaller chunks, making and constantly revising plans, constant testing, and sheer determination. It was absolutely not perfect, but with a combination of teamwork, 10 diagrams scrawled on lined paper, a function that was really 12 or so nested lists, and a 4 hour session in the library, we had done it. That feeling of satisfaction and pride we felt in our work was immense. 

Experiences like this are what have drawn me to engineering and computer science. The feeling I get when I've solved a puzzle like this one is always what keeping drawing me back. And now, I am excited to use those skills to help out this community!

In groups of three to five, we were required to go through the process of product development, starting with contacting clients, producing a minimum viable product, and finally presenting our product in front of a panel of experts in the industry.

After reaching out to multiple clients, my group ultimately worked with JoAh Academy, a newly founded test prep academy that provided 5-12th grade extra-curricular learning services and college consulting. Our client was looking for a way to digitize their processes as they fully operated on paper, including grading and testing. They asked us to focus on three main tasks – a new home website to act as a central hub for their clients, a testing environment to simulate digital standardized exams, and facilitated communication between students and teachers. By the end of the year, my group had created a home website as well as a dashboard system for students and teachers. Teachers/Admin would be able to create short quizzes as well as longer PDF exams, send announcements to students, administer new students, and read inquiries sent from the main website. Students would be able to read announcements and take short quizzes or PDF exams. Our tech stack involved Django, SQLite, Bootstrap, and GitHub.

Because this was our group's first time building a large scale project and working heavily with web development, we struggled a lot with time management, directory organization, and even choosing a tech stack. Setting realistic expectations and presenting problems to our non tech-savvy client proved to be difficult as well. Another big challenge was working with databases and learning about security, including penetration testing! Through all these problems, with trial and error, teamwork, and time, we were able to get through all these challenges and produce a super cool project.

column16: The project I am most proud of is my creation of an AI model that can learn how to improvise jazz music over a set of chord changes. This was my introduction to the world of generative music, which is an emerging field involving music created through algorithmic composition. In research of this topic, I discovered music21, a tool created for computer-aided musicology. The extensive documentation for music21 became my guide, but I soon realized the holes in my programming knowledge. Every line of code became a quest for answers as I sought to create a Markov model: a simple model that used probabilities to determine the next musical note in a generated composition. However, a major challenge was finding a dataset that my model could learn to train off of. With no musical jazz dataset online, I had to create my own dataset by transposing different jazz albums and converting them into a MIDI(a music file readable by programs). After doing this, I was able to build a simple Markov Model by following tutorials online that learned to improvise music based on a chain of probabilities. After successfully finishing the project, I explored more current models, such as neural networks, capable of crafting nuanced jazz improvisations and learned to construct my first deep learning model. After seeking help from a mentor who specialized in AI music generation, we were able to create a working LSTM model that learned to improvise jazz using Keras. As my curiosity grew in this topic, I created my own jazz metrics using theoretical concepts from my musical background to help better quantify how well our models were actually learning to create jazz. Based on my music theory knowledge of jazz, I was able to create two novel metrics which I wrote a paper on and eventually presented my work and got it published at an IEEE multimedia conference.

column16: One of my favorite projects I worked on was in my second year of high school. For my AP Computer Science class's final project, I decided to create a Chess AI. To do this, I first had to program chess. Surprisingly, the game itself wasn't as complicated. I built the game by utilizing a 2x2 matrix, with the locations of each piece stored in the matrix. For each piece, I created a child class to define their unique movements. The hardest part of the project was the Chess AI. Since I had no experience with machine learning at the time, I didn't know how to train a model. Instead, my approach was to use recursion to loop through all possible moves for 3 layers of potential moves. The AI would then grade each move and then make the move with the highest grade. One of the hardest challenges I had with this was determining an algorithm for grading each move. I decided to implement a system where each piece had its own value. Pawn would have a value of 1, bishop a value of 3, etc, with the king having the highest value. Since the AI only looked 3 layers into the future, I prioritized the moves that could take the highest value piece from the opposing team while losing the least value. Although there are still some things I could improve on, it is still one of the projects I am most proud of as it is the first large-scale project that I coded.

One project I'm especially proud of is a centralized certificate management system I worked on during my time at Amazon. Our team faced challenges with managing certificates—renewals were often manual, and if missed, they could lead to service disruptions. To address this, we brainstormed as a team and designed a system that could automate certificate lifecycle management, improve visibility, and reduce the operational load on the team.

Before I even started implementing the system, we spent time discussing the requirements and sketching out how it would fit into our existing infrastructure. It was a collaborative effort where everyone contributed ideas on what tools we could leverage and how to handle the different renewal timelines for various services. Once we had a solid plan, I took the lead in building the system using AWS tools like Lambda and DynamoDB. The system not only automated certificate renewals but also provided notifications to make sure that nothing slipped through the cracks.

One of the biggest challenges was making sure that the system was flexible enough to handle different services’ unique renewal needs. I worked closely with the team to ensure we were setting up notifications and monitoring that aligned with each service's requirements. The fast-paced environment meant I was constantly participating in code reviews, debugging, and testing, but I enjoyed that aspect because it pushed me to write high-quality, maintainable code.

In the end, the project reduced our team’s workload and increased service reliability, which was incredibly satisfying. It was exciting to work on something with such a direct impact, and it gave me the chance to deepen my experience with AWS technologies while collaborating closely with my team.

column16: One project I’m particularly proud of is the Bayesian Model for Sports Prediction that I worked on during the ACE++ program at Tufts. The project aimed to predict the Boston Celtics' probability of winning based on whether they played at home or away, using Bayesian analysis. We collected real-world data from the Celtics’ 2023-2024 season, including their win-loss record and home vs. away performance, and developed a model that adjusted prior beliefs based on new data. One of the biggest challenges we faced was incorporating multiple priors, such as coach experience and player performance, into the Bayesian equation. We tested different statistical distributions to fine-tune the model, and this process enhanced my understanding of Bayesian analysis and gave me valuable hands-on experience with data modeling and Python coding. It was an exciting project that allowed me to combine my passion for sports with my technical skills.

A small group of friends and I participated in the GMTK 2024 Game Jam over the summer. It was a 96-hour competition to make a video game based on the theme "built to scale." The game we created was about a kid and a robot who solve puzzles and float around using a balloon that can puff up to get comedically huge. We used Unity, which uses C#, as our engine, and to collaborate we used GitHub Desktop and Git Bash. The game jam was tough, but ultimately very fun and memorable. I definitely came out as a stronger collaborator and programmer than how I came in. We also placed just outside of the top quartile out of 7,615 submissions.

This was my first time programming on a medium-sized team (5 people). The experience was super educational; I learned a lot about how to communicate, cooperate, and plan with a group of developers. I also worked alongside an artist and a musician who had little/no programming experience. Working with individuals with diverse skill sets in a fast-paced setting also helped me develop better communication skills, learn from other’s expertise, and enhance my ability to collaborate efficiently in a creative environment. Together we acknowledged each others' strengths and weaknesses, learned how to allocate our tasks rationally, and combined our skills to create a final product.

It was challenging to learn how to use GitHub Desktop 'on the job,' but it pushed me to adapt to a new and highly useful method of digital collaboration. Making a full-fledged game in a short timespan alongside people with unique abilities led me to learn other new things quickly (for example, various new Unity features and new algorithms for terrain generation) and evaluate important questions under pressure (should I implement this feature, how should I do it, how do my time constraints affect me, etc.).

Now, after my experience working with developers in a group setting, I am excited for my next opportunity to do it again.

column16: One project that I am really proud of was a script that I and a lab PI created over the summer at a Linguistics lab I was working at. The project was to extract data to be statistically analyzed from speech audio samples through the program Praat. The goal of the project was to rework the language production model. The study was set up in a way that participants were given different phrases to read out loud in order to illicit speech errors. The data I was working in was in the form of audio clips that were transcribed and segmented through using features in Praat. Individual words were isolated as well as syllables and the frequency of each sound. There were over 60 participants and for each one we were looking at certain syllables that were targeted. Each participant individually had about 300 targeted syllables in their speech samples and 7 types of data needed to be extracted for each syllable that was targeted. We worked in Praat's scripting program to create the script and this proved to be very challenging. The language was very counterintuitive and was missing a lot of key features that python and C++ have which made the coding process very challenging. The language syntax was also incredibly bizarre, certain variables were in double quotes and some were in single quotes but they never established which one was meant for what in their scripting tutorials online. Safe to say it consisted of a lot of trial and error. To start we created a table that contained the participants speaker ID and the 7 types of data we were looking for from each individual syllable. From there we created a list to hold all of the text grids (a name for the files that have the audio samples in them). From here we iterated over the text grids one by one, retrieved the speaker ID and then determined which syllable we were looking at. This part proved to be the most challenging because of the way the experiment was set up. The specific syllables or sounds we were interested in were S and SH. The sentences participants were supposed to repeat were a word that started with neither S or SH, then a word starting with S then a word starting with the sound SH. For example peach seek chic. Originally our idea was to create a counter, so every time we encountered a syllable that was neither S or SH we started it at one. Then the next syllable was S and that was count 2, and then SH was three and then once it hit there it restarted and looked for the next syllable that was not S or SH. This worked at the beginning but then we came to realize that sometimes the participants were not completing the statements fully or repeating words when they shouldn't have. This made the count off and the statements were all jumbled when we tried to extract them and the target syllables were not maintained. So if someone had said peach seek seek chic this would be counted as a sentence twice, once with each seek. Ideally this sentence would not be counted tho as we did not want to include any sentences that had errors. We debated going through and fixing all of the data processing to throw out any instances where the participants messed up an utterance but that would've taken an incredibly long amount of time. We went through a lot of trial and error with this case but ultimately we created a for loop to iterate through the tier (similar to a list) of syllables. If a SH was found then we called a function that was able to extract the length of the syllable, the Center of gravity of it, and much more. From there we started counting back wards and went one interval back from the SH. Then we had a while loop that kept moving back one syllable until it found an S or it had gone back 4 syllables (if the participant had said the sentence correctly that's the max amount it would have been back from the SH syllable.) Then we called the same function as with the SH to extract the necessary data from it. We also had other checks to make sure the SH wasn't at the beginning of the list cause otherwise you couldn't start counting back from it, and to check that the pausing between the words were not too long (then the speech error would not be vaild). After this we had to extract the sentence that matched with each syllable we extracted data for. (if we were looking at the data from the S syllable you would want to know which sentence it came from so you would extract "peach seek chic" with it). For this we did something similar as looking for the syllables. We checked that the first syllable was not S or SH, if it was then we appended it to a table and then had a series of counters for repetitions to get the sequence extracted correctly. (I attached the link to the script below and it has comments explaining the process more indepth). Finally we appended all of the data into the same sheet. The whole process was pretty challenging, working in a new and very outdated programming language created a lot of issues. There were many times where we were wishing we were using python. One big challenge we had was the time and space the program took up. Praat requires you to create new objects every time you try and extract a piece of sound data (which we had to do for finding the center of gravity) so by the end of the program we had over 12,000 objects that were created in the Praat object list (user interface) so we had to add in code to delete these. If we would have known about it's memory and space issues we should have designed a more efficient program but we were on a deadline so we could not restart, and in the end the program did run and work perfectly.  The whole experience was super rewarding I really enjoyed having a real way to put my coding skills to use, it was my first coding project outside of CS11 or CS15. I also really loved getting to work with my lab PI the collaboration and brainstorming that coding projects require is so much fun. I really love working with other people on these types of assignments.

I developed an AI-powered tool to help users search for human movements in 2021. I made this because I love drawing but I was really bad at drawing people, so I created a tool to help me find reference pictures for the poses I wanted to draw.
I was inspired by a 3D spherical joint doll model and decided to use 12 human joints to create a 2D stick figure. My goal was to create a product that matches photos in a training dataset with the pose of the stick figure. 
Although a few years ago, there wasn’t an AI craze like what we saw in 2023. I managed to find an AI tool called Mediapipe Pose to analyze 3D human movements using different joints. 
New to machine learning, I worked with a mentor who introduced me to “K-Means Clustering,” an algorithm for image analysis. The recommended photos, however, did not match my stick figures at all. 
Disheartened, I tried to debug by comparing joint angles within images, but nothing worked. Inspired by trigonometry during a calculus class, I decided to develop my algorithm, which I later published in GitHub as “difference between angles.” By incorporating the trigonometry value of the angles and fine-tuning my model, I managed to achieve an accuracy rate of  87 percent for the matching results.
To provide artists worldwide easy access to my tool, I taught myself HTML and JavaScript to publish my tool online using a web user interface. 
A few months later, I was really happy to hear from people like me who wanted to learn drawing that they thought my tool was helpful.

Last year, I was part of "TomAgro", a branch of TOM (Tikkun Olam Makers) where our aim was to help farmers with small productions make their operations more productive, so they could better compete in the market. I was part of "Team Yeison", where we worked to develop a WhatsApp chatbot to help Yeison in processing orders from his clients, helping him optimize his current system. In this project, I was directly involved in the programming, which centered around using AWS and WhatsApp Business Management API to develop a chatbot that could take orders and store them in a database, making it easier for Yeison to process orders and organize his schedule for delivery. Costumer would be presented with a catalog, and they would be able to place orders directly within WhatsApp without the need of intervention from Yeison's end. The orders, along with the delivery location, would then be stored in a Google Sheets file, where Yeison could easily see the orders he needed to pack. This way, he could better plan his trips into the city and optimize his process. Additionally, the costumer had the option to get a weekly reminder to place an order.

TomAgro consisted of a main event lasting three days during which the projects are to be built. Leading up to the event, my team and I met on several occasions with an expert in WhatsApp chatbots from the company Bonnet Analytics. We then learned the bases of AWS and WhatsApp Business Management API, as well as practiced coding with Python. We also learned to use Postman, as we would use it to send requests and test our bot. Learning to use new platforms was definitely of the biggest challenges I faced. The project took a while to begin, and I had very little time to thoroughly learn all the tools we would be using. When the main event started, I felt unprepared, and every task seemed a bit overwhelming. However, within the first hours I got much more familiar with how the tools worked together and the team soon fell into a rhythm. We got to learn about using message templates from the WhatsApp API, outputting data to a database, using AWS to run our code, etc. It was trial and error, and those three days were long, but by the end of the third day we had a product we were proud of. Fortunately, Yeison loved it.

column16: I really enjoyed working on arith, a pair-programming project for CS40 where my partner and I had to work under tight deadlines. I didn’t know my partner prior to the project, so we had to quickly align our schedules and working style, which was a challenge in the beginning. Working on the project involved a lot of planning forward and breaking down the problem into sub-problems. I took the lead on the main structure of the program and implementing the core compression algorithm using color space transformations. Thanks to planning forward, we got everything done before the due date (after almost camping in JCC <3). We ran into a problem when doing one last run right on the day the project is due, where our program could not work on the largest files. Thanks to having a clear project structure, we had a clear idea of where things could have gone wrong and soon found out the problem was that we did not clear the cache and we had multiple copies of the gigantic file which ended up messing up everything else. We screamed into the void, cleared the cache and it ended up fine. So although not the most large-scaled project I have worked on, arith helped me learn the importance of planning forward and gave me a chance to actually begin to enjoy the process of collaborating with other people, looking for resources and asking for help. I love CS40. And TAs.

column16: In my junior year of high school, my group and I developed a Discord bot that simulated the game of Blackjack for our computer science class’ final project. To put our project on Discord, we imported a library called Javacord, allowing us to create buttons that the user could click and listeners that responded to the user’s actions. For actions within the game like shuffling or hit/stand/double down, we used Java but tweaked it a little using Javacord. We also implemented a user’s balance and betting system that was stored in a JSON file to simulate winning and losing money. One big challenge we faced was learning enough of Javacord to implement everything, which meant reading through the documentation, understanding the code, and then applying it to our code. The documentation was confusing but luckily I had a skilled coder on my team to navigate the process. Another problem we faced was underestimating how much time we had to complete the project. In the beginning, we worked bit by bit during class time making sure everything ran smoothly. But by the last couple of days, we realized we needed to pick up our pace and started working on the project outside of class, which meant rushing code and hours of debugging. Overall, this four-week project provided a valuable learning experience. Collaborating with a skilled coder at my table proved invaluable as I learned from his code and his thought process. He also clarified the confusing aspects of the code such as the function of different Listeners and how to store data in a JSON file. My high school did a competition every year called the Hallway Competition. Based on the grade’s class color (ours was green) you decked out a hallway in that color with a theme. Each grade went all out to decorate their hallways to reflect their unique personality and spirit. In freshman year we really did not know what we were doing and ended up coming in last place because we had no leadership or a solid plan. 

The next year I was elected Co-Lead of my class' planning committee. Unfortunately, my classmates were deeply divided on the idea of a jungle theme, and I knew we wouldn't be successful without wide agreement. Convincing everyone to trust a singular vision was difficult and tiring but absolutely required. It allowed us to pull off the most realistic fake jungle I have ever seen. We won by a landslide, but more importantly the whole grade worked together towards a common goal, and learned to truly collaborate.

In junior year, mid-way through the competition, I was unexpectedly sent home due to a COVID-19 exposure. While I was disappointed that I could not physically be with them, they demonstrated that great things can happen when everyone works together. It became an opportunity to unite and for new leadership to emerge. Students called me for design input and virtually showed me progress. Witnessing my peers work together to make an amazing hallway was exactly what I wanted. I was proud of our grade's enthusiasm and amazing teamwork. This collective work resulted in another victory!

By the time senior year rolled around practically everyone in the grade wanted to help and we ended up with an amazingly colorful hallway (complete with a 10 foot high foam cave). Even though the contest might have been trivial and just a fun way to get into school spirit, it was truly an amazing experience. It helped me become a better leader and learn how to collaborate while also having fun and doing what I love.

column15: Although my first formal introduction to computer science was CS11 at Tufts, I would be lying if I said that’s what piqued my interest. In my senior year of high school, I had to complete a 50-page thesis as a part of the Global Studies program. I was originally set on researching an International Relations topic, since that had been my interest for years. However, I was inspired by a previous student’s choice to write about baseball stats despite his similar area of study. I chose to complete my thesis on the impact drafting has on an NHL team’s success, and spent the next five months diving deep into a world of statistics, spreadsheets, and t-tests. I found myself working on even the most boring parts of the paper at 11pm when I didn’t even need to, thinking about it in my free time, and looking forward to the next time I could open my computer and contribute to the Excel sheet again. This project sparked my interest in data and computer science and is the true reason I chose to begin taking CS courses at Tufts and eventually decided to major in computer science.
column16: At the beginning of this school year, I overheard a friend of mine, Jake Flosi, talking about how much time he and his fellow JumboCasters spend looking for statistics for their games. I began thinking about ways to automate it but immediately ran into a wall when I realized I needed to learn web scraping. I sat down the next morning for half an hour and watched a couple of YouTube videos, then, with increasingly difficult sites, I practiced my skills until I got up to the Tufts Athletics site, starting with the volleyball section. It had much more complicated HTML and the data points I was scraping were all stored in different ways, but eventually, I was able to create a basic Pandas data frame with the volleyball player information. From there, I got to work building different pathways of data to grab, starting with defensive volleyball stats, moving on to separating overall and conference stats, and then adding soccer. After that, I added a functionality where you could choose which year you wanted to look at and different ways to parse the data (per player, per stat, with certain conditions, etc). I returned to Jake with what I had, and he asked me two important questions. First, can I access other schools, and second, how do I work with this? I realized that I hadn’t implemented any kind of interface a user could use to pull all the data I’d scraped. After building that, I looked into the HTML of other NESCAC schools’ sports pages and realized that every website was built the same, so my code already worked on it. Lastly, I looked over my code and noticed it was incredibly inefficient, so I condensed much of the code into modular functions that could work with multiple sports. I invested many hours into this project, but it never felt like work due to my passion for sports. Although I was unfortunately never able to fully complete it, I enjoyed every moment of the experience and learned a lot from it.

Thinking from the users’ perspectives, I make sure the feedback I provide can guide the users in the right direction and give hints about how close they are. I also make sure the game responds appropriately when the input is invalid (non-numeric value or exceeding the number limit). One challenge I have met was thinking from the users’ perspective when coding the games and giving clear instructions. column16: One project I'm really proud of is a Remote Procedure Call (RPC) program I wrote in class last fall. The project consists of a Python program that generates a C++ client and server pair. The client initiates a Remote Procedure Call of a function by sending the function information to the server, the server then executes the function and sends back the result, which the client then reports, all via generated code. The project required a lot of pre-planning to figure out how we were going to generate the code and how we were going to set up our generation system to be adaptable for all different kinds of data types, including nested structs and arrays. I had also never previously coded in Python, so I was learning on the fly. The project taught me a lot about how to plan, specifically plan in a way that will be scaleable. Sometimes you have to do something in a "less efficient" way in the beginning in order to make it more efficient and elegant later on. CalendarConnect:
   I have a project called CalendarConnect. The main goal of the project is to help better connect university students from different schools with an easy-to-use calendar. We all know that academic calendar websites are annoying, hard to read/compare, and are not in a calendar format for some reason. On CalendarConnect all you have to do is enter the university names of the schools you want to see on your calendar and then the breaks, start date and end dates, and exam periods all pop up on your calendar. It is currently still in partial development however a beta version is currently deployed to the web with only about 30 schools (including Tufts, many Boston schools, other top schools, and many schools that my friends go to lol). 
How I made it:
   I used React and chakraUI for my front end, Node.js for my backend, selenium in Python for web scraping the academic calendars, and then GitHub and Vercel for organization and deployment. A big challenge that I faced was web scrapping the academic calendars, especially in bulk. Websites have all different variable names, organization, and other features that make it very hard to create a generalized webscrapping script. What I did was I created a JSON file with specifics to each website such as span class with the proper info, paths to find buttons, etc. and then I created a Python script that went through the JSON file and took the necessary data for webscrapping the given urls inside the JSON file. I also tried other methods such as scrapping basically all of the information from the website and then filtering it. Right now I am in the middle of trying to find the best and easiest method of doing this before I go and try to get 1000 universities or so.

During the last summer, I had worked on a personal project with my 3 other friends. The motivation was: we are all in a Vietnamese Tech Community. Everyone in the community are all very supportive and willing to give out referrals to help people in need. Usually, people who can be a referrer will comment or make a post to notify others about that. Then, candidates (people who need referrals) will inbox the referrers, hoping that they would get a respond soon. This process is very time-consuming and frustrating for both party: the referrers have to go through all of their messages and read through all of the resumes sent to them, then set up the meeting with people who they think could be qualified, etc.; the candidates also have to wait to until the referrers get to their message, or maybe will never get a response since the referrers have filled up their referral slots. So, my friends and I decided to create a web app that can automatically match candidates with the opened referring slots, which fastens the referring process as well as reduce the frustration for both parties.
My responsibility then was in both front end and back end. In particular, I mainly worked on file storage solution, notification microservice, and some other front end components.
To be honest, I was really struggled, especially in the first few weeks, as I never had any experience building a web application before that. I remember myself spending hours reading the documents and watching multiple youtube videos just to understand how I could use OAuth and LinkedIn API for authorization (we wanted to connect the user's account with their linkedin!). Things actually got better as I understood more about how everything works. I gradually got myself bigger tickets like implementing both front end and back end of a user form, storing user files to S3 bucket; designing and implementing the notification microservice utilizing AWS Lambda, SQS, SES, Firebase; writing reducers for front end logic, etc. (Have to credit my awesome teammates here -- they helped me a lot! always opened for discussion and gave me so many advices, which helped me learn wayssss fasterrr!!)

column16: For my high school senior project, I worked with a non-profit organization that focused on providing clothing and hygiene items to underserved communities in the area to redesign their ordering system to stock their hygiene kit making station. When I started, there was no information about what items were most desired or how many of each item were being distributed each month. I started by creating an online form for volunteers to track item distribution amounts. I did face some challenges with having volunteers consistently and accurately complete the form. So, I started taking inventory of all the in stock items during my shifts and then estimating the daily distribution based on these numbers instead. I then compared these results to the survey to confirm overall accuracy. I also created and carried out a survey that asked people about their most desired items. I compiled all this data collected over a month into a spreadsheet and determined which items were most essential. I also performed an analysis of the cost to try to minimize any unnecessary expenses. This was also difficult because some of the preferred items were expensive. For example, many people preferred the travel size secret deodorant that was occasionally offered instead of the cheaper non name brand travel size deodorant. I put an emphasis on trying to offer nicer products when they were in high demand and less nice products that were in low demand. At the end of a month period, I proposed a monthly ordering plan that was approved by the organization, and then I put all of the items on auto order so the hygiene station would always be stocked.

Though this project does not reflect my skills as an actual programmer, it is by far the most rewarding because I get to see the impact it makes on a community I care about, and continues to be used today by Conversations to Remember.

As the Student Outreach Coordinator for the program, I was responsible for overseeing new and returning volunteer sign-ups, matching students with specific patients, and scheduling calls with specific facilities. Similar to the problem LCS Tutoring currently faces, we were managing all of our sign-ups via google form but as the program expanded, coordinating all the information became unmanageable. As an eager high school junior, I was ready to jump into the project with virtually no technical experience. Paired with two (actually experienced) developers, we worked as a team to improve the sign-up system. Because the developers were not volunteers themselves, it was up to me to clearly identify and communicate the necessary features to implement. 

Based on the feedback I had received from my trainees, having a single form for both new and returning volunteers was both confusing for the students and coordinators. To solve this problem, we created two separate forms, integrating the new-volunteer form in the website, while sending out the returning volunteer form in a separate email.

The biggest challenge of our project was the transition from Zoom to Jitsi, a smaller online meeting platform. When we test-launched the new platform, students were struggling to download the Jitsi app and had a hard time signing into their calls. To combat this, we got rid of the need to download the app by integrating the meeting platform into the website, where volunteers could log in directly with their personalized meeting code. However, after relaunching, we discovered that volunteers (especially Zoom users) were struggling with the transition to a web browser and had difficulty finding the login portal. Finally, after much reworking, we realized that the best way would be to sidestep the login process entirely, and just allow volunteers to connect directly from the home page of the website.

Although I was not heavily involved with the actual programming of this project, it taught me valuable lessons on how to not only identify problems, but also how to effectively address them through communication, teamwork, and critical thinking. I hope that through JumboCode, I will be able to get the opportunity to apply my newfound knowledge of CS to similarly impactful projects.

This project was the result of many years of experience coding with my best friend Sameera Murthy, as part of the Congressional App Challenge for our district, MA06 with Representative Seth Moulton. 

Climate change is a really important issue to me. Looking back at my Google Photos from years ago, I see videos of my younger self playing in the Massachusetts snow in December, making snow angels and laughing my heart out. There are pictures of me with my parents in New York City, enjoying the vibes of the snowy city during winter break. The arrival of spring is hard-earned and unexpected. Nowadays, New England is warming faster than any other region in the United States, and spring comes faster with no snow to enjoy. This is not the life I want to be living.

My solution? Create an app that, even in our busy day-to-day schedules, allows users to take small steps to keep track of their carbon emissions in order to reduce our global carbon footprint. This app was intended for anyone, young or old, who wanted to make an impact to stop the climate crisis.

This project was made with months upon months of hard work, planning, creating a design on Figma, and arguing. Our biggest difficulty that we spent a while on was finding the right framework to use for our code. Progressive Web Apps are websites that are compatible to be apps on both iPhone and android. We tried using React at first, as well as Nuxt, but these frameworks only complicated the process. Then, we bumped into Svelte, which allowed us to easily make reusable components while keeping simplicity in our code. It also allowed us to integrate the Progressive Web App system with no difficulties. On a personal level, me and my friend disagreed very often on how the coding structure would work and how the app would even function. We had arguments for hours on how the buttons should be placed and how even something as simple as an svg should appear.

In the end, our app won first place for our district for the Congressional App Challenge and we were presented with a Congressional Recognition certificate in addition to an invitation to the prestigious #HouseofCode event in the U.S. Congress this year. We were able to meet our state representative Seth Moulton, and our app is currently being framed in the U.S. Capitol. This was an experience I will never forget in my life, and I am really proud of how my coding experience helped me create something truly impactful, even recognized on a congressional level.

Before my high school graduation, I founded the "Arise and Shine" support group, which started as an emotional outlet and evolved into a thriving center for mental well-being. During my time with "Arise and Shine," I met Naila, a 12-year-old girl whose dreams of education were stifled by her tribe's entrenched tradition of early marriages for girls. 

To help Naila and other children in her village, I initiated an outreach-tutoring program with support from dedicated teachers and fellow students. We made bi-weekly visits to Naila's village, offering vital academic support to the local children.  

Initially, we faced resistance from parents in the village. However, with the assistance of group members from the same tribe, we worked to change their perceptions of our program. We emphasized how education could empower Naila to support herself and her family, offering an alternative to the traditional bride price of 20 cows. Eventually, we obtained permission for Naila to resume her primary education.  

Naila's graduation and acceptance into a nearby secondary boarding school filled me with immense pride and gratitude. Her journey has become a powerful symbol of the transformative potential of education. Her success, alongside other talented, marginalized girls I've had the privilege to support, has further fueled my determination to make a difference in the lives of those facing similar challenges.  

Jumbocode's mission,  which emphasizes community service, feels like my new home  away from "Arise and Shine." My goal is to continue advocating for education, empowerment, and mental well-being in underserved communities. Together with like-minded individuals, I'm committed to leaving a lasting impact and ensuring everyone has a chance to rise, shine, and fulfill their potential.

column16: I am proud of my research with the Hassoun Lab, where I led a project on leveraging pre-trained, search-enabled LLMs to automate and improve biological data retrieval. I independently built an end-to-end retriever using Python, gained experience using packages such as Pandas, Numpy, Langchain, OpenAI and RDkit, and learned a new tech-stack (primarily docker, git, RESTful APIs and jupyter). Through my research project, I uncovered that although there is potential for search-enabled LLMs to outperform manual searches, there is a long way to go. I built it using Python, leveraging tools such as BioPython, OpenAI API, Pandas, dotenv, CSV and JSON to handle biological text data processing. Planning what data to use, how to extract it from KEGG, and accessing it via the Entrez API was a big challenge. There was a vast amount of data, and much of it was was missing or irrelevant. I had to utilize big data management and data structures strategies to store, organize, and access compressed data through streaming. In addition, I learned to use the natural language processing tools needed to preprocess this textual data. My work thus far has led to my first major achievement: the submission of an article, Evaluation of search-enabled Pre-trained Large Language Models on retrieval tasks for the PubChem Database, to the JCIM. One project that I am proud of was the app that I had built during my summer internship at Bristol Myers Squibb. After visualizing the workflows for one of the team’s business processes, I realized that there were several bottlenecks characterized by a lot of manual work, which led to a lot of time being wasted. 
I had proposed developing an app to reduce manual data entry, but my idea was initially rejected as the team did not want to adjust their workflow due to the technical learning curve. My goal was to gather data and assess how much time was being spent on manual processes like managing documents and inputting data so that I could highlight the potential benefits of an app that could automate much of their tasks.
To tackle this, I gathered data that measured the inefficiencies of the current workflow, tracking key performance indicators such as the time spent on document processing and delays in information retrieval. I also worked closely with team members to get a better understanding of their workflow and the pain points they faced. After collecting and analyzing the data, I created visualizations to specifically show the team members where the bottlenecks were. Based on my research, I was able to present my findings to the team, who ultimately agreed that an app would be helpful to address some of their pain points. I was able to build the app for them, which would allow them to handle shipments from external vendors as well as manage their data that had been manually entered into their other systems, ultimately reducing up to 10 hours per week of manual work. 
One of the most rewarding aspects of this project was seeing how analytical and empirical research could be leveraged to convince a group to change their mindset. I think that one of the biggest challenges in working in a team is to convince someone to accept a new way of doing things, and being able to let the team see that there was an alternative that would benefit them was something I found fulfilling. This project not only allowed me to apply and expand my technical skills but also gave me a sense of accomplishment in contributing to a solution that could benefit business and reduce complexity.

column16:
I built a website for the New Jersey Astronomical Association to help them better plan their public events! The problem I solved for them is very hard to illustrate, so in short: the observatory has a telescope whose vision is blocked at certain angles and at certain times. They wanted me to create a system calculates what angles work or don't work so that they know what to use during demos with the public! 

To solve this, I first took a manual data points that corresponded to when exactly the vision got blocked. I made two excel sheets with all of this data—it took about two months to collect. Secondly, I found a best fit line and extrapolated an equation. I then coded my first website from scratch, hosted on Glitch.com, to utilize this equation. Languages I used include CSS, Java, JS, HTML. Essentially, it prompts the user for their desired telescope angle, and then returns how long to wait until the telescope is usable at that angle.

Some issues I encountered was learning how to make the UI interface friendly. Though it's still not perfect, it's much improved. I solved this by making many text size changes, adding color contrast, and adding borders to buttons/inputs for better readability. I found that neatly placing/organizing my website elements via centering/alignment was especially hard and is something I'm looking to improve.

All in all it was a great first project and showed me how fun coding is, especially when you're creating it to solve a problem for someone else! When I presented it to them I felt really fulfilled and I hope to extend that concept here at JC.

1) My grandfather was a farmer. Every summer (and some winters - though it wouldn’t be the season), we’d go to my paternal grandparents’ house in a small city in east Turkey. My grandfather had a small piece of land that he inherited from his own father, where he (and my dad and uncles when they were children) harvested apples and apricots from a few trees. These fruits would later be divided into two groups: those to go to juice factories (i.e. those fruits that weren’t pretty enough to sell) and those to go to the farmers’ market. I’d then go with my grandfather and my cousin to yell “1kg for only 5 lira!’ at the market and look cute to elderly ladies to sell some apples and apricots. However, most of our work involved keeping track of all the trucks and boxes coming in and out, understanding who gave us what and what we gave back in return. While keeping track of all these, we’d also continue holding tight to the cash money on our small hands. We’d save all the money in little boxes and my grandfather, with his limited education and even more limited math, would try to understand how much he actually sold. My cousin and I then would use our 4th grade star-earning math skills to multiply, subtract, and divide to find out the exact kilos and exact liras we sold, lended, or left aside. He’d then carry all these boxes in his small car where we’d barely fit as two small children. It was a really messy work with (looking back) a great loss of efficiency and profit but to me, at the time, all this work seemed like the most innovative and efficient of them all. I was very happy to put my 11-year-old-skills to use to help my grandfather.

I never had the opportunity to use my highschool math skills, or my finance skills, or my marketing skills that I developed over the years to help my grandfather - as we lost him the year I started highschool.

During my senior year of high school, I participated in a team of three as a developer for a video game project that we submitted to the Future Business Leaders of America state competition. The prompt that year was a "word-based" video game, so my team and I first discussed what kind of game and what the game mechanics would look like. We came up with an idea that amalgamated a lot of ideas from previous games we had all played. Our game's premise ended up being that a player would collect letters as they appeared and moved on a track in front of the player. Then, the player would have to spell words with those letters they collected to earn points. For the project, our one teammate created original art for the game graphics and assets. My other teammate and I used the Godot game engine to organize the game into scenes and to implement the game mechanics. 

The first challenge I faced while participating in this project is that I had never coded a video game before or used Godot. There was definitely a learning curve for me while creating the game. I started out just adding background music to levels, then moved on to placing buttons and creating new scenes, and then eventually moved on to creating and editing algorithms for the game. When we presented the project at the Future Business Leaders of America NJ State Leadership Conference, we won first place for the project and moved on to the National competition! It felt so surreal, realizing that we had taken our project from ideas and thoughts on a page to a playable product that won a competition.
