This summer, while scratching my head trying to figure out what my schedule would look like, I decided to implement a topological sorting program to help me plan out my academic career. This was my first ever personal project; I still remember the thrill of completing it, suddenly realizing that I have a range of programming toolkits at my disposal to assist me through hardship. 
I went into the planning stage only knowing the general features of a topological sort algorithm. One of the first struggles I encountered was how to establish the graph – since to the human eye, nodes with pointers was the best representation, I attempted to use a complicated linked list. This soon failed, as this approach was messy and the program had to cluelessly jump between nodes trying to find the starting point. After some research I chose an adjacency matrix holding Boolean values as the final representation. Another difficulty was finding a data structure to help the computer decide which node to go next in the sort, and queues was the best solution. 
During the testing phase, I had accidentally put in a cyclical dependency in my graph, causing me infinite agony. This experience taught me the importance of using a debugger and tracing through code by setting stop points. Overall, this project had gave me a boost in confidence and desire to create more practical programs. I became familiar with a branch of algorithms I originally had no experience with and inspired me to continue exploring other programs (I am currently trying to implement a pet quokka class).

At the end of the competition period, the top scorers were rewarded with gift cards. We also "hired" a group of students in charge of digging through the trash cans during lunch periods to remove recyclable items from them and put them in their proper bins. In the end, our goal was to turn a seemingly boring series of assemblies and seminars into an engaging continuous event that actually had students participating in environmental justice! Last semester, for my ES2 final project we were prompted to choose any topic and a dataset(s) about that topic, then analyze and visualize it. For this project, I utilized the Python libraries pandas, NumPy, and Matplotlib for data manipulation and visualization. 

First, I chose my topic and datasets. My focus was healthcare accessibility across racial groups, specifically in my lovely home state of Connecticut. I compiled demographic and health-care related data from the Connecticut Health Care Survey and the American Community Survey from 2012-2013, and added all the information I was going to use in a dataframe, which was divided into separate dataframes by race. Then, I isolated and calculated key metrics, such as the percentage of individuals unable to afford prescription medications, and visualized these alongside median income estimates by race using grouped bar charts. I repeated this process to visualize the percent of people who did not receive health care due to cost worries by race. 

A challenge that I faced was assessing bias in my analysis. My analysis could be biased in the sense that starting out, I had expectations for what results I would find. This could have caused confirmation bias by influencing which information and questions I chose to include in the analysis. Perhaps if I decided to investigate responses to different questions from the Connecticut Health Care Survey, I would have found my predictions proven wrong. In part to prevent confirmation bias and in part to ensure that there was enough information to draw valid conclusions from, I chose which information from the survey to explore by looking at whether there were adequate responses to the question. To further prevent this I could have randomly chosen which questions I looked into. 

After my analysis I concluded that race and median income does play a role in the disparity within health care accessibility. For example, race groups with a higher income had a lower percentage of individuals unable to afford prescription medications. Overall, it was really interesting to focus on something that I consider important and in my home state. I really enjoyed creating something mostly of my own accord without strict requirements, like those characterizing many of the projects we do in CS classes.

One project I’m particularly proud of is Gerp, a program designed to search through files and find patterns based on regular expressions, similar to a simplified version of the Unix grep tool. It was my first experience with paired peer programming, and that dynamic introduced a new set of challenges. Collaborating effectively with my partner meant learning to balance our approaches and communicate frequently to solve problems efficiently.
The technical aspect that was particularly challenging was implementing hash tables. I understood them conceptually, but applying them to manage large sets of data with optimal time complexity was more difficult than anticipated. The need to manage memory efficiently and write a solution that would handle real world, large datasets without significant performance drops became a central focus. Debugging, testing edge cases, and ensuring the program’s accuracy were also challenging but rewarding.
We built the program through consistent iteration—testing small parts of the system, refining how the hash table interacted with the rest of the program, and working to ensure it would work accurately and handle different types of regular expressions and file sizes. This project helped improve my skills in working with data structures, optimizing for performance, and working collaboratively to solve complex coding problems.

I'm probably most proud of the first personal project I worked on, which was a database containing various information about different tennis players. I'm a pretty big tennis fan, so it was a fun project to get an initial feel for different parts of programs that I didn't experience outside of cs classes. I learned how to do a lot of error checking and data validation to ensure that everything I imported from the official websites came across correctly and was in a readable format.

For the actual project, I got some hands on experience with C++ and data structures in general. For getting the information, I tried some various web scraping techniques, but I got most of the information by manually inputted information into a file to read in from. I used a hash table to both insert and search for players with the key being the player or tournament name, depending on the information I wanted. I used a different class as a value for things like their height, weight, whether they used a one or two handed backhand, etc, and a second hash table for tracking their head to head matchups against other players. I kept track of their matches and head to heads against opposing players, and other information like their ranking or prize money earned. I kept some other information like the tournaments played in a simple vector in order of when in the calendar year they are played. I faced a lot of challenges related to data validation and updating it with more recent information, but I'm mainly happy because it was a great experience to really get a better understanding of different ways to do the same thing and parsing through a lot of data. I had a lot of trouble figuring out how to store the information outside the running program, so I had to export it to various files and try to read it in again to see what could work.

It was honestly a super fun experience to just learn coding outside of a structured environment with no stakes and at my own pace, especially about something I am really interested in. It was also probably the first project that I really planned out and debugged alone outside of class homeworks, so that was another cool part of it for me personally.

A project that I am proud of is my final project for CS20. We were tasked with creating a web app that served a useful purpose. We decided to create a project that consolidates a wide variety of recipes. Users could filter through these recipes based on their nutritional values and look through the ingredients they required. I am always on the hunt for a good recipe, so this project was really fun to do! To ensure that everyone was on the same page about the layout, I started by creating a rough sketch of how we wanted our website to look, which we then transferred to Figma. 
     We made a lot of progress using HTML/CSS and Javascript to lay out the initial structure of our website along with completing the static pages. At this point, the challenges started to appear. We were having a lot of trouble implementing our API into our website. This required us to deep dive into the API’s documentation and review lots of stack overflow posts. After significant troubleshooting, we were able to use JQuery and Javascript to get it to work. The next big challenge we faced was using Node.js to set up a user authentication system. We used MongoDB to get a user’s login credentials but there was some trouble with distinguishing between someone who may have subscribed to our service and someone who had not. In the end, we ended up simplifying the distinction between the two and were able to finish our project. I am proud of how our website turned out and it was really fascinating to be able to see how far we came from the rough sketch I had initially made on the back of my recitation worksheet.

One of the most exciting projects I worked on was during my internship at a startup this past summer. It was my first time working with a development team, and since it was a small group, I had a lot of freedom to take charge of the project. At first, it was a bit overwhelming—I didn’t have any prior professional experience, and I had to figure out a lot on my own. But I quickly realized this was a great chance to step up and really make the project my own.

The main focus of my project was processing and analyzing data from machine-learning models. This data came from job postings in the clean energy industry, covering things like salaries, benefits, and required skills. My job was to automate the data processing using Python, which I wasn’t too familiar with at the time. The learning curve was steep, but after some serious trial and error (and a lot of Googling), I started to get the hang of it. 

One of the biggest challenges was dealing with messy, unstructured data. The job posting data wasn’t exactly neat, so I had to get creative in cleaning it up and making it usable for analysis. I built scripts that not only processed the data but were also designed to be reusable for future projects, which saved a ton of time in the long run. By the end of it, I had set up automated data pipelines that made the whole process much more efficient. 

As I was wrapping up the data work, I noticed that people were having trouble digging through endless Excel sheets to find specific insights. I suggested building a simple web app to make the data easier to access for both the team and stakeholders. My manager was on board but given the scale of the project we settled on focusing on just salary and benefits, and I spent the rest of my internship building this web application.

I used Flask and SQLite to build the app—nothing too grand, but it made sense for the small scale of the project. The trickiest part was designing an interface that was easy to follow, but after a few iterations and feedback from the team, I came up with something that worked well. In the end, I delivered both the data pipelines and the web app, which ended up helping many people within the company. 

Looking back, this project was very rewarding because I could see the direct impact of my work. I learned a lot along the way and came out of the experience feeling more confident in my skills.

One project I’m particularly proud of is Gerp, a utility designed for searching text files within a directory hierarchy, much like the "grep" command in Linux. Gerp reads all files in a specified directory recursively and stores their contents in a hash table for efficient searching. 

I worked on the project through pair programming. It was also my first time programming with a partner, which turned out to be a really enjoyable experience. Pair programming gave us the chance to learn from each other’s different ways of thinking. It wasn’t just about getting through problems faster—it was about exploring different approaches and fine-tuning our solutions together. It made the whole process feel more engaging and rewarding, and it definitely improved the quality of the final product.

One of the hardest parts of building Gerp was planning for efficiency, especially given the scale of the project. Since Gerp had to recursively read through large directories of text files, it was crucial to consider the time complexity of the algorithm. Managing the algorithm's efficiency was essential to ensure that the program could scale well and handle large datasets without crashing or suffering from poor performance.

As with any large-scale project, debugging presented its own set of challenges. Despite our extensive planning, we encountered persistent bugs, especially when dealing with edge cases in larger directories. To address these issues, along with unit testing, we also created custom input files to thoroughly test edge cases, ensuring Gerp’s functionality across different scenarios. Additionally, we used Valgrind to detect memory leaks and other potential issues, ensuring that the program ran efficiently and reliably without memory mismanagement.

Overall, working on Gerp was a deeply rewarding experience that strengthened both my technical skills and my ability to collaborate effectively on complex projects.

column16: This past summer, I interned at a startup that provides software to manage audiology practices, and one of the most exciting projects I worked on involved developing a new tagging system for providers. The task was to enable practice-level management of tags, allowing providers to create their own filters for patients, which was crucial in improving their workflow. Technically, I started by updating the existing Tag model to make it more flexible. This involved removing and adding new fields. I also had to extend our API to support listing, creating, updating, and deleting tags. This meant implementing filters that allowed users to fetch either verified global tags or tags created by their practice. Additionally, when a tag was no longer needed, I had to implement a system where the tag could be deleted if unused, or dissociated from the practice if it was shared across multiple practices. One of the main challenges I faced was ensuring data integrity while adding the flexibility needed for practice-level management. For instance, I had to ensure that the verified field defaulted to True for existing tags while allowing new tags to be unverified, and I needed to manage cases where multiple practices might use the same tag. Another challenge was designing the UI for the new tags management page, which needed to align with existing settings pages and provide a user-friendly interface for administrators to manage their tags. Despite the complexity, it was incredibly fulfilling to build something I knew would make a real difference for our users, helping them manage their practices more efficiently. This project excited me because it wasn’t just about implementing features—it was about solving real-world problems that impact people’s day-to-day work. The best project I've been on is the water automation system at EWB (Engineers Without Borders). In this project, we had three groups to set up an automation system for the plants in the Tufts greenhouse. I helped in the electrical group. The hardest problem of the project was communicating between groups. Our electrical group was responsible for coding the motors and the pump to feed water to the plants according to each plant’s necessary water intake. We had to make an interface for students to put in plant watering information. I was also responsible for the wiring for the system. We had to connect the wiring such that each motor would run depending on which plant needs watering. This was extremely rewarding because I had to learn a little bit of everything. From 3D printing to soldering, I learned a lot of skills for the whole project to come together. It was rewarding to see all the pieces I helped work on slow being brought together. It was almost miraculous that everything worked in the end.


The most challenging part of the project was easily the work across groups. Our group relied on every other group to work, and vice versa. As such, we were often forced to make changes to fit the confines of another group’s design. For example, the motors that I initially wired were too weak to move the water gates; As a result, I had to change the motors which caused us to completely redesign our wires and our coding. This project taught me the key to success in a project is communication. If one group was kept in the dark, no group would have succeeded— each group excels with the help of others.

One of the coolest projects I had the pleasure to work on was actually something me and 3 other friends created during a hackathon. Our project “MyVoterInfo” was a web app designed to target voter suppression by providing up-to-date information ranging from the user’s registration status to nearby ballot locations, polling hours, and more. 

The user’s voter status was scraped from the state’s online public voter registration website using Puppeteer (given the limited time, we were only able to set it up for the state of Massachusetts), and a lot of the location data was sourced from the Google Civic API (a very cool find!). We integrated all this information with the Google Maps API to allow the users to see the various locations relative to their own home address. 

In terms of the actual process, our awesome co-lead was able to set the barebones React Native framework before the start of the competition. From there, the designer of our group made awesome POCs and wireframes as the rest of us went off to do some research on what resources we could use. This included finding the right APIs, learning more about the style library that we were using, and overall getting familiar with the React Native framework. And then from there, we moved on to the implementation steps.

As someone who had more experience with the frontend side of things, I went about setting the API calls for the Google Civic API and started implementing the various components and layouts that my designer friend had created. My other two friends went about setting up all the backends and tirelessly fixed any last minute bugs before our demo time. 

All in all, the 2-day project was a huge success! Our demo went smoothly and we even went home taking the big prize! (Overall Winner!!) In retrospect, I wished I polished up my backend skills more and familiarized myself more with the framework since the biggest challenge we had was debugging when we began combining the various components. Additionally, given such a short timeframe, we had to sacrifice some functionalities in order to focus on our primary features. So, taking this all into consideration, when I begin my next project, I hope to bring both a solid technical background and a strong sense of organization and prioritization (plus a cheerful spirit) to ship a product from its early development stage to deployment!

I believe that one of the truly effective ways to improve the lives of others is active help. It’s not enough to take action within a bubble of comfort, such as sympathizing with a cause - an action has to be taken for compassion to be meaningful. 
My first real step out of my comfort zone was during quarantine. Actually, it was more of a sprint. 
Cut to me walking in the smoldering heat, hanging posters on the fences, bulletin boards and bus stops as the tape slipped through my sweaty fingers and the stack of paper occasionally pierced my skin. 
I had decided to host a food drive, despite being the definition of an introvert. On the day of the food drive, I nervously waited under my school’s entrance, listening to the drumming of rain. My doubts dissipated as car after car pulled into the driveway, and with every donation, I remained incredulous that people had come to support a rogue food drive organized by a freshman. But when I advertised my food drive in my Zoom classes, emailed my English teacher whom I’d never met in person to sponsor it and asked the school for a table, words flowed out of me in waves. 500+ food items were collected and on the drive to the food pantry, I knew I had fallen in love with community involvement. 
 I realized that I was worried people wouldn't show up because, in all honesty, I was unfamiliar with the US and the city that I called home for the past six years. I decided to get to know my new community better and signed up to be a camp counselor at the Jewish community center across from my house. The unfamiliar faces became family as I danced the mornings away with the entire camp, learning how to celebrate Shabbat with challah and grape juice every Friday. The exhaustion after entertaining competitive eight year olds was worth every minute when I got to know their personalities and stories.
Involving myself in my surrounding community has helped me understand that even the smallest actions can help someone and motivates me in dedicating my career to aiding those in need.
In partnership with the county executive’s office, I helped organize Middle Eastern American Heritage Month celebrations and when I saw the astonishment on guests’ faces, marveling that the government saw their heritage as worthy of celebration, I felt even more motivated to continue engaging in community work. 
Last summer, I tutored English at a children’s house in Almaty, Kazakhstan. Initially, it was really hard to find any organization that offered volunteering opportunities and upon that discovery, I started calling place after place looking to be useful and using my English knowledge for good. When I eventually found a home willing to let me teach, it was some of the most rewarding tutoring I have yet performed. 
After witnessing my goals come to fruition as a result of my passion and commitment, I’m only further imbued to experiment with ideas ahead of me and my future team.

One project I’m really proud of is an interactive currency-exchange app called currentc.wiki that I helped create during the Wellesley hackathon. The app provides real-time exchange rates between two currencies, displays a one-month historic rate graph, and even evaluates whether the current rate is favorable. Our goal was to build something practical that could help people make more informed decisions about when to exchange currencies (which was inspired by my struggle with reloading Flywire everyday to figure out the best exchange rate to pay my tuition).

We built the app using a prediction algorithm powered by a Python-based backend and Shiny’s GUI system to keep the interface simple and intuitive. I worked on the web-based components using Web Assembly, which was a challenge but ultimately improved the app’s speed and performance. One of the biggest technical hurdles we faced was scraping the currency data efficiently, and me and my team solved this by using regular expressions to handle large sets of data. Throughout the process, we used GitHub for version control to manage updates and keep everything organized, and we successfully deployed the app as a fully interactive website.

What made this project exciting for me was not only solving technical challenges but also seeing how the app could be useful in the real world. It ended up winning three awards at the hackathon, including “Most Readily Employable” and “Best Financial Hack” with Capital One, which was really rewarding after all the hard work we put in.

column16: For my internship last summer (2023), me and two other interns built a API microservice application to automate dataset summary and improve search for NASDAQ DataLink! Before this project, all of the one line summaries for the datasets were done manually. These summaries were then fed into the search algorithm, so they were resulting in poor search results. We started completely from scratch, designed our own architecture, tested a bunch of different text-summarization LLMs (ChatGPT, Falcon40B, and T5, to name a few), and then spent the last couple weeks of the internship getting our application deployed. The main challenge we faced was that we were given almost no direction with this project, so right from the gate we had to pull together whatever combined knowledge the three of us had from classes and past experience to make something that none of us had ever done before. We also had to figure out how to delegate amongst the three of us, and play into our individual skills to get the project done in the 10 weeks we had. We started the application having only one service (just a Flask app), but then realized about halfway in that, because of the way we had delegated the project, we could have three distinct services and turn the project into a microservice application. One of the services communicated with Databricks, which hosted the model. The second one (the one I worked on) communicated with Gitlab API, which would use a Gitlab Webhook to trigger our summarization every time an update was made to the dataset repo. The third acted as a "master" service, and also facilitated the front end of the application. We actually ended up finishing ahead of schedule, and decided to take on the challenge of trying to deploy our service. Only one of us had ever worked with Docker before, and none of us had done anything with Kubernetes before, so this involved a lot research and asking for help. Besides this, we were also able to add some bonus features (such as keyword generation) to also feed into the search algorithm and further improve results.

Over the summer, I was a fellow in the Make-A-Play Program, which is designed to help under-represented athletes gain professional experience. For the second half of the fellowship, the fellows were divided into six groups for a case competition, where we were given a business problem that we needed to solve and present on. I was selected as the “scrum master” of my group, and was in charge of planning our meetings, delegating tasks, and essentially ensuring everything came together at the end. I was completely brand new to this kind of work, as it was essentially a consulting project (we had to come up with a budget, a KPI framework, a risk assessment, etc), and there were a lot of moving parts. We all agreed on the phases we were responsible for, and we scheduled weekly meetings to go over our progress. One issue we ran into was that a lot of the content we were responsible for was unclear, and when we sent out messages to the company, they did not respond. So, it was up to us to investigate and complete additional research to ensure we were going in the right direction. One big challenge I faced was when one of our group members stopped responding one week before the presentation. I worked with another group member to complete his part and we ended up getting everything done in time. 

This project was the first time I was the leader of a real-life business project, and it taught me a lot about leadership, teamwork, and problem-solving under pressure. I learned how to manage unexpected challenges, communicate effectively with a team, and take initiative when things didn’t go as planned. Despite the obstacles, I was proud of how we pulled together and delivered a successful presentation. This experience gave me confidence in my ability to lead and adapt in a professional setting. After our presentation, all of my group members texted in the group chat about how proud they were and how they appreciated me “keeping everything together.” Of course I was incredibly proud of the outcome, but hearing that my group members enjoyed being a part of our team and felt that I had done a good job leading was the most rewarding part of the experience. It reassured me that not only had we delivered a solid project, but I had also created a positive and supportive team environment.

Last semester for Engineers Without Borders, me and another member of my tech group were tasked with building a temperature and humidity sensor using arduino for the greenhouse. The first challenge we faced was finding an arduino sensor that works as the first few that we bought produced worrying results (99999 degrees fahrenheit). By reading many reviews of sensors and forums we eventually found a sensor that was not only effective but also fit our budget. Once we found a sensor that worked, we had to code the sensor to fit the arduino as the arduino we were given was not the one that the sensor was meant for. It took many meetings to code the sensor correctly, we encountered many linking errors, compiling errors, and errors we have never heard of before which were especially frustrating as there are no office hours for club projects. After countless hours, we eventually got the correct temp and humidity to be displayed in the terminal, now how do we display that in the greenhouse? We scoured through Nolop to find a lcd display (that we were allowed to use) and had to figure out the correct wiring to display what the terminal was outputting onto the display. I have minimal experience working with wires so it was a lot of fun learning about circuits hands on. By the grand opening of the greenhouse we got the sensor up and working for everyone to view!

I am very proud of this project as it was my first time working on a programming related project outside of school and the fact that it will be playing a part in teaching sustainability to others excited me even more!

column16: Last summer, I created a website for Tufts Conference & Event Services (CES) to be able to easily view and loan furniture on campus for various events they organize. This project was super interesting and challenging to me because before that, my only experience with web programming was taking CS20 (Intro to Web Dev). I got to learn and use technology I had never used before: React.js for the frontend, Node.js & Express.js for the backend, and MySQL for database. My biggest challenge by far was piecing together all these different technologies to connect the frontend to the backend, and the backend to the database; I learned from watching many Youtube videos of people doing full-stack web programming. I implemented features allowing users of the site to view, create, and update the furniture inventory, work orders, and CES event details. To connect the backend to the database, I ended up using an ORM called Sequelize to convert the tables from mySQL database into objects that could be more easily manipulated using JavaScript. This was a super cool aspect of the project to me because I did not even know that it was possible to do that. To connect the frontend and backend, I learned to make API calls.
